title: Nullspace and homogeneous directions
terms: nullspace; null space; kernel of a matrix; nullity of a matrix.

exposition.text:
n
For an m × n matrix A, its nullspace is N (A) = {x ∈ R : Ax = 0}. It is a subspace of the input
n m
space R , not generally of R . Solve the homogeneous system by elimination and express the
answer as a linear combination of vectors multiplying independent free parameters.
Those parameter vectors form a nullspace basis; their number is the nullity. Row operations
preserve the nullspace because they preserve solutions. A square matrix is invertible exactly
when its nullspace is {0}, but a rectangular matrix can also have trivial nullspace when its
columns are independent.
2
For a square matrix, ker A ⊆ ker A ⊆ · · · , since another application of A still sends zero to
zero. These inclusions can be strict; a vector may map into the kernel without itself being in
the kernel.

solution.text:
The equations are x + 2y + z = 0 and y + z = 0. Let z = t, giving y = −t and x = t. Thus
the nullspace is spanned by the nonzero vector (1, −1, 1).

question.text:
What is the nullity of the 4 × 4 matrix whose every entry is 1?
(A) 1 (B) 0 (C) 4 (D) 3 (E) 2

solution.text:
All rows are identical and nonzero, giving rank one. The kernel consists of vectors whose
coordinates sum to zero, of dimension 4 − 1 = 3.

If ker A ∩ ker B = {0} for maps A, B : R → R , which map is injective?
(A) A − B (B) x 7→ (Ax, Bx) (C) B (D) A + B (E) A

solution.text:
The kernel of the stacked map is exactly the intersection of the two kernels, which is trivial
by hypothesis. Cancellation can prevent A + B or A − B from being injective.
